t: LeetCode 1486 — XOR Operation in an Array
o: We must XOR together the n elements of an implicitly defined array where nums[i] = start + 2*i. For example, n = 5, start = 0 produces [0, 2, 4, 6, 8] whose XOR is 8, and n = 4, start = 3 produces [3, 5, 7, 9] whose XOR is also 8. Since each element comes straight from a formula, no array ever needs to be allocated. The small constraints (n <= 1000) make a direct loop instant, but the regular step-2 structure also supports an O(1) closed form built on the period-4 pattern of XOR prefixes.
k: The array is fully determined by n and start — XOR elements on the fly instead of materializing nums.
Because the step is 2, every element shares the parity of start; factoring out 2 reduces the problem to XORing consecutive integers.
The XOR of 0..x cycles with period 4 ([x, 1, x+1, 0]), so the XOR of any integer range is computable in O(1).

a.i: Compute each element from its formula and fold it into a running XOR. This is literally what the problem statement describes and is more than fast enough for n <= 1000.
s: For i from 0 to n-1 compute nums[i] = start + 2*i.
a.t: O(n) — one pass over the n generated values.
a.sp: O(1) — only an accumulator is kept.

a.i: Write each element as 2*h_i + (start & 1) where h_i = (start >> 1) + i runs over consecutive integers. The high bits of the answer are therefore the XOR of the range [h, h+n-1] shifted left by one, and the low bit is (start & 1) repeated n times. Using the period-4 rule for prefix XOR, the range XOR is prefix(h+n-1) XOR prefix(h-1), evaluated in constant time.
s: Let h = start >> 1 and define prefix(x) = 0 ^ 1 ^ ... ^ x via the pattern [x, 1, x+1, 0] indexed by x mod 4.
Compute R = prefix(h+n-1) XOR prefix(h-1), the XOR of consecutive integers h..h+n-1.
a.t: O(1) — a handful of constant-time evaluations independent of n.

w: Open with the simulation — interviewers expect the straightforward pass first, then offer the O(1) formula as a bonus. Pitfalls: miscounting the low-bit contribution when n is even (odd count of odd terms only), and shifting before masking in fixed-width languages. Edge cases: n = 1 returns start itself; start = 0 makes every element even so the answer is always even. Likely follow-ups: XOR of an arbitrary arithmetic progression, or replacing XOR with sum modulo something.
